# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Учитель**
Transliteration: oo-CHEE-tyel  
English meaning: teacher  
Example sentence: Мой учитель говорит по-русски.  
Example translation: My teacher speaks Russian.  
Memory hook: Imagine your teacher cheering “You can do it!” — the “cheer” sound in “учитель” helps you remember the friendly guide at school.  
Repeat after me: учитель… (pause) учитель.
- Russian (Cyrillic): школа
  Transliteration: SHKO-la  
  English: school  
  Example sentence: Я иду в школу.  
  Example translation: I am going to school.  
  Memory hook: “School” starts with the same “shk” sound as “school” in English — easy to remember!

- Russian (Cyrillic): урок
  Transliteration: oo-ROK  
  English: lesson  
  Example sentence: Урок начинается в девять.  
  Example translation: The lesson starts at nine.  
  Memory hook: “U-rok” sounds like “you rock” — your lesson rocks when you learn!

- Russian (Cyrillic): книга
  Transliteration: KNEE-ga  
  English: book  
  Example sentence: Учитель читает книгу.  
  Example translation: The teacher reads a book.  
  Memory hook: Picture a “knee” holding a “ga” (book) on your lap while reading.

- Russian (Cyrillic): писать
  Transliteration: pee-SAT  
  English: to write  
  Example sentence: Дети пишут в тетради.  
  Example translation: Children write in a notebook.  
  Memory hook: “Pee-sat” sounds like “pea sat” — the pea sits and writes.

- Russian (Cyrillic): читать
  Transliteration: chee-TAT  
  English: to read  
  Example sentence: Я читаю книгу.  
  Example translation: I read a book.  
  Memory hook: “Chee-tat” like “cheetah” racing through pages fast.

- Russian (Cyrillic): ручка
  Transliteration: ROOCH-ka  
  English: pen  
  Example sentence: Дай мне ручку, пожалуйста.  
  Example translation: Give me a pen, please.  
  Memory hook: A “rooch” (pen) fits in your hand like a little “ka” friend.

- Russian (Cyrillic): класс
  Transliteration: KLAS  
  English: class / classroom  
  Example sentence: Класс большой и светлый.  
  Example translation: The class is big and bright.  
  Memory hook: “Klas” sounds exactly like “class” in English!

- Russian (Cyrillic): друг
  Transliteration: DROOK  
  English: friend  
  Example sentence: Мой друг сидит рядом.  
  Example translation: My friend sits next to me.  
  Memory hook: Your “drook” is the buddy who “drums” up fun at school.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Today we look at the verb “читать” (to read) in the present tense. Russian verbs change endings depending on who is doing the action.  
- Я читаю (I read)
- Ты читаешь (you read)
- Он/она читает (he/she reads)
Unlike English, which often keeps the verb the same (“I read, you read”), Russian adds different endings so the listener instantly knows who is acting.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: школа**
No way — the Russian word for school started life meaning “free time”! It began in ancient Greek as skholē, which first described leisure or spare time for thinking and discussion. Greek scholars passed it to Latin as schola, then it travelled into Old Russian around the 17th century through Western European languages. But be careful — in English we also say “school,” yet the Russian version kept the original Greek “skh” sound while English softened it. Here’s a memory trick: picture Greek philosophers relaxing in their skholē, then suddenly deciding to turn their free time into a classroom — that same peaceful spot became школа!

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, the first day of school on September 1 is called “День знаний” (Knowledge Day). Children bring flowers to their teachers and the whole school gathers for a special assembly to celebrate the start of the new learning year.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a picture of your classroom and label three things using today’s words (учитель, книга, ручка).  
For adults: Imagine you are meeting a new Russian classmate — introduce yourself and say one thing you like about school using at least two new words.

> **Today we meet some wonderful Russian animal words that will help you talk about the creatures all around us, from tiny birds to big bears.**

### Word of the Day
**пингвин**
Transliteration: PEENG-veen  
English meaning: penguin  
Example sentence: Пингвин плавает в воде.  
Example translation: The penguin swims in the water.  
Memorable hook: Imagine a penguin waddling like a little black-and-white tuxedo bird!  
Repeat after me: пингвин… пингвин.
- Russian (Cyrillic): птица
  Transliteration: PTEET-sa  
  English: bird  
  Example sentence: Птица летает в небе.  
  Example translation: The bird flies in the sky.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “tweet” — perfect for a bird!
- Russian (Cyrillic): рыба
  Transliteration: RY-ba  
  English: fish  
  Example sentence: Рыба плавает в озере.  
  Example translation: The fish swims in the lake.  
  Memory hook: Think of “river” but shorter — fish live in water.
- Russian (Cyrillic): заяц
  Transliteration: ZA-yats  
  English: hare  
  Example sentence: Заяц прыгает быстро.  
  Example translation: The hare jumps quickly.  
  Memory hook: “Zayats” sounds bouncy, just like a hopping hare.
- Russian (Cyrillic): волк
  Transliteration: volk  
  English: wolf  
  Example sentence: Волк живёт в лесу.  
  Example translation: The wolf lives in the forest.  
  Memory hook: “Volk” is close to “folk” — think of wolf packs like a folk group.
- Russian (Cyrillic): медведь
  Transliteration: med-VYED'  
  English: bear  
  Example sentence: Медведь ест мёд.  
  Example translation: The bear eats honey.  
  Memory hook: “Med” means honey, so медведь is the “honey-knower”!
- Russian (Cyrillic): корова
  Transliteration: ka-RO-va  
  English: cow  
  Example sentence: Корова даёт молоко.  
  Example translation: The cow gives milk.  
  Memory hook: Remember our review word корова from before — it moos “ko-ro-va”!
- Russian (Cyrillic): собака
  Transliteration: sa-BA-ka  
  English: dog  
  Example sentence: Собака бежит быстро.  
  Example translation: The dog runs fast.  
  Memory hook: “Sobaka” sounds like “so bark-a” — dogs bark!
- Russian (Cyrillic): кошка
  Transliteration: KOSH-ka  
  English: cat  
  Example sentence: Кошка спит на окне.  
  Example translation: The cat sleeps on the window.  
  Memory hook: “Koshka” is cozy like a cat curled up.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Russian nouns have three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter. Most animal words ending in a consonant are masculine (like волк), words ending in -а are usually feminine (like корова), and some ending in -о are neuter. Examples: Волк большой (The wolf is big — masculine). Корова большая (The cow is big — feminine). This is different from English, where we don’t change adjectives for gender.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: медведь**
This word started in ancient Slavic languages as a clever way to avoid saying the real name of the bear, which people once feared. It literally breaks down to “med” (honey) + “ved” (knower), so it means “the one who knows honey.” Russian speakers used this polite nickname instead of the older word for bear. But be careful — the English word “bear” comes from a completely different root meaning “brown,” so it’s a false friend in sound and meaning. Here’s a memory trick: picture a bear sniffing out honey like a detective who always finds the sweet stuff.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russian fairy tales, the bear is often a strong but kind character who lives in the forest and helps or tests the hero. Russians love stories like “Masha and the Bear,” where the bear is big and a little clumsy but friendly.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your favourite animal and say its Russian name out loud three times while colouring it. For adults: Look around your home or neighbourhood, point to any animal (even in a picture or on TV), and say the Russian word for it in a full sentence like “Это собака.”

> **Today we open the door to the warm, everyday words Russians use to talk about the people closest to them.**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**мама**
Transliteration: MA-ma  
English meaning: mom  
Example sentence: Моя мама любит чай.  
Example translation: My mom loves tea.  
Memory hook: It sounds almost exactly like the English “mama” — the first word many babies say everywhere!  
Repeat after me: ма-ма… мама.
- Russian (Cyrillic): папа
  Transliteration: PA-pa  
  English: dad  
  Example sentence: Папа читает книгу.  
  Example translation: Dad is reading a book.  
  Memory hook: Just like “papa” in English — easy to remember!

- Russian (Cyrillic): брат
  Transliteration: brat  
  English: brother  
  Example sentence: Мой брат играет с собакой.  
  Example translation: My brother is playing with the dog.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “brat” but means the opposite — a helpful brother!

- Russian (Cyrillic): сестра
  Transliteration: ses-TRA  
  English: sister  
  Example sentence: Сестра любит цветы.  
  Example translation: Sister loves flowers.  
  Memory hook: Starts with “ses” like “sister.”

- Russian (Cyrillic): бабушка
  Transliteration: BA-bush-ka  
  English: grandma  
  Example sentence: Бабушка печёт пирог.  
  Example translation: Grandma is baking a pie.  
  Memory hook: Say it like “ba-bush-ka” and picture a cozy grandma baking.

- Russian (Cyrillic): дедушка
  Transliteration: DYE-dush-ka  
  English: grandpa  
  Example sentence: Дедушка рассказывает историю.  
  Example translation: Grandpa is telling a story.  
  Memory hook: “Dye-dush-ka” — the “dye” part sounds like “dad” plus “ushka.”

- Russian (Cyrillic): сын
  Transliteration: syn  
  English: son  
  Example sentence: У меня есть сын.  
  Example translation: I have a son.  
  Memory hook: Short and strong, like the English “son.”

- Russian (Cyrillic): дочь
  Transliteration: doch’  
  English: daughter  
  Example sentence: Дочь рисует картину.  
  Example translation: Daughter is drawing a picture.  
  Memory hook: Ends with a soft “ch” sound — say it gently.

- Russian (Cyrillic): ребёнок
  Transliteration: rye-BYON-ok  
  English: child  
  Example sentence: Ребёнок играет в парке.  
  Example translation: The child is playing in the park.  
  Memory hook: “Rye-byon-ok” — think of a little “rye” bun that is your child.

- Russian (Cyrillic): родители
  Transliteration: ro-DI-te-li  
  English: parents  
  Example sentence: Родители любят детей.  
  Example translation: Parents love their children.  
  Memory hook: “Ro-di-te-li” — the people who “rod” (give birth) to you.

- Russian (Cyrillic): тётя
  Transliteration: TYO-tya  
  English: aunt  
  Example sentence: Тётя приезжает в гости.  
  Example translation: Aunt is coming to visit.  
  Memory hook: “Tyo-tya” sounds bouncy and friendly, just like a fun aunt.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, family words often change slightly depending on who they belong to. We use “мой” for “my” with masculine words (мой брат) and “моя” for feminine words (моя сестра). It works like English “my,” but you must match the ending to the word’s gender. Example: Мой папа (my dad) vs. Моя мама (my mom). This small change makes your sentences sound natural and correct.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: брат**
This word started in the ancient Proto-Indo-European language spoken thousands of years ago as *bʰréh₂tēr. It travelled through Slavic languages and arrived in modern Russian unchanged in its core sound. English “brother” comes from exactly the same ancient root, so the two words are true cousins! But watch out for the false friend — in some Slavic languages “brat” can also mean “buddy,” which might surprise English speakers. Here’s a quick memory trick: picture two brothers sharing a “brat”wurst at a family picnic — the shared sound helps you remember they mean the same thing.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, families often gather for big Sunday lunches where three generations sit together. Grandparents (бабушка and дедушка) are very involved in raising children, and it is common for adult children to visit their parents every weekend.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your family and label each person with the new Russian words (мама, папа, брат, etc.). For adults: Introduce your family out loud in Russian — “Это моя мама. Это мой папа.” — and say it three times. Remember поезде from a few lessons ago? Now try: Моя семья едет на поезде!

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Одежда**
Transliteration: a-DYEZH-da  
English meaning: clothes / clothing  
Example sentence: У меня есть новая одежда.  
Example translation: I have new clothes.  
Memory hook: Think of “a-dye-zh-da” like “a-dye-zh” – you dye your clothes different colours!  
Repeat after me: О-де-ж-да… одежда.
- Russian (Cyrillic): рубашка
  Transliteration: roo-BAHSH-ka  
  English: shirt  
  Example sentence: Я ношу синюю рубашку.  
  Example translation: I am wearing a blue shirt.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “roo-bash-ka” – imagine a rooster wearing a bashful shirt!

- Russian (Cyrillic): брюки
  Transliteration: BRYU-ki  
  English: trousers / pants  
  Example sentence: Мои брюки чёрные.  
  Example translation: My trousers are black.  
  Memory hook: “Bree-oo-ki” – think of “brew-key” trousers you wear while brewing tea.

- Russian (Cyrillic): платье
  Transliteration: PLAT-ye  
  English: dress  
  Example sentence: Девочка носит красивое платье.  
  Example translation: The girl is wearing a beautiful dress.  
  Memory hook: “Plat-ye” sounds like “plat-yeah” – a plate of pretty fabric!

- Russian (Cyrillic): обувь
  Transliteration: O-boov'  
  English: footwear / shoes  
  Example sentence: Моя обувь удобная.  
  Example translation: My shoes are comfortable.  
  Memory hook: “O-boov” like “oh, boov” – boots that make you boogie!

- Russian (Cyrillic): носки
  Transliteration: nas-KEE  
  English: socks  
  Example sentence: Я покупаю тёплые носки.  
  Example translation: I am buying warm socks.  
  Memory hook: “Noss-key” – socks that hold the key to warm toes.

- Russian (Cyrillic): куртка
  Transliteration: KOORT-ka  
  English: jacket  
  Example sentence: Зимой я надеваю куртку.  
  Example translation: In winter I put on a jacket.  
  Memory hook: “Court-ka” – a jacket you wear to court (or just to stay warm)!

- Russian (Cyrillic): шапка
  Transliteration: SHAP-ka  
  English: hat / cap  
  Example sentence: Надень шапку на голову.  
  Example translation: Put a hat on your head.  
  Memory hook: “Shap-ka” sounds like “shap-cap” – a shapely cap!

- Russian (Cyrillic): ботинки
  Transliteration: ba-TEEN-ki  
  English: boots / shoes  
  Example sentence: Ботинки на ногах.  
  Example translation: Boots are on my feet.  
  Memory hook: “Ba-teen-ki” – teeny boots that make you teeny-tiny steps.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, adjectives must match the noun in gender, number, and case. For clothing words, this means the ending changes.  
Examples:  
- синяя рубашка (blue shirt – feminine)
- чёрные брюки (black trousers – plural)
- удобная обувь (comfortable footwear – feminine)
Unlike English, where adjectives stay the same, Russian adjectives “agree” with the noun – a fun pattern once you notice the endings!

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: куртка**
This word started in French as “jacket” (jaquette) and travelled into Russian in the 18th century when French fashion words flooded in. But be careful – the Russian “куртка” sounds nothing like the English “jacket” even though they share the same root! The surprise is how many clothing words Russian borrowed from French during Peter the Great’s time. Here’s a memory trick: picture a French courtier handing you a “court-ka” jacket – the sound stays in your head forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians often wear a шапка (hat) and валенки (felt boots) in winter because the cold is serious business. Brightly coloured scarves and gloves are common gifts, and children learn early to say “Надень шапку!” from their babushka.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw yourself wearing three new items and label them in Russian (рубашка, брюки, шапка).  
For adults: Look in your wardrobe and say out loud “У меня есть…” + three clothing words you see.

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Дом** (dom)
Pronunciation: dohm (rhymes with “home”)  
English meaning: house or home  
Example sentence: Мой дом большой.  
English translation: My house is big.  
Memory hook: Think of “dom” as the dome that shelters your whole family — your own little kingdom!  
Repeat after me: Дом… дом.
- Russian (Cyrillic): комната
  Transliteration: kom-na-ta  
  English: room  
  Example sentence: В комнате есть стол.  
  Example translation: There is a table in the room.  
  Memory hook: “Com-na-ta” sounds like “comfy nook” — the perfect spot to relax at home.

- Russian (Cyrillic): кухня
  Transliteration: kookh-nya  
  English: kitchen  
  Example sentence: Мама готовит на кухне.  
  Example translation: Mom cooks in the kitchen.  
  Memory hook: Imagine “cook-nya” — where the cooking magic happens!

- Russian (Cyrillic): окно
  Transliteration: ok-no  
  English: window  
  Example sentence: Я смотрю в окно.  
  Example translation: I look out the window.  
  Memory hook: “Ok-no” comes from “oko” (eye) — the window is the eye of the house.

- Russian (Cyrillic): дверь
  Transliteration: dvyer’  
  English: door  
  Example sentence: Открой дверь, пожалуйста.  
  Example translation: Open the door, please.  
  Memory hook: “Dvyer” sounds like “dear” — the door you open for dear friends.

- Russian (Cyrillic): стол
  Transliteration: stol  
  English: table  
  Example sentence: Мы едим за столом.  
  Example translation: We eat at the table.  
  Memory hook: “Stol” is where the whole “stole” of family stories is shared.

- Russian (Cyrillic): стул
  Transliteration: stool  
  English: chair  
  Example sentence: Сидите на стуле.  
  Example translation: Sit on the chair.  
  Memory hook: “Stool” is almost the same in English — easy to remember!

- Russian (Cyrillic): кровать
  Transliteration: kro-vat’  
  English: bed  
  Example sentence: Я сплю в кровати.  
  Example translation: I sleep in the bed.  
  Memory hook: “Kro-vat” — crawl into your cozy “crib-vat” at night.

- Russian (Cyrillic): лампа
  Transliteration: lam-pa  
  English: lamp  
  Example sentence: Лампа светит ярко.  
  Example translation: The lamp shines brightly.  
  Memory hook: “Lam-pa” lights up your “lamp-a” corner of the room.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, we use the preposition “в” (in) with the prepositional case to say where something is. For example: В комнате (in the room), на кухне (in the kitchen — note the special ending for кухня). Compare to English “in the room.” Russian changes the ending of the noun, while English usually stays the same.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: окно**
This word started in ancient Slavic as “oko,” meaning eye, because a window lets light into the house just like an eye lets light into the body. It travelled through Old Russian and kept its simple form while English “window” came from a completely different phrase meaning “wind eye.” But be careful — the Russian “око” is an old poetic word for eye, not the everyday “глаз.” Here’s a memory trick: picture the window as the house’s watchful eye, always open to the world outside.

**Cultural Corner:**
In many Russian homes, the kitchen is the heart of family life where people gather for tea and long talks, even more than the living room. Guests are often welcomed straight into the kitchen, showing that warmth and hospitality matter more than fancy furniture.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your dream Russian home and label three rooms in Russian (комната, кухня, окно).  
For adults: Walk through your own home and name each room out loud in Russian — “Это кухня. Это моя комната.”

> **Today we’re strapping on our рюкзак and jetting off to master Russian travel words that turn every trip into an adventure!**

### Word of the Day
**путешествие**
Transliteration: poo-tesh-ESS-tee-yeh  
English meaning: journey or trip  
Example sentence: Я люблю путешествие на поезде.  
English translation: I love a journey by train.  
Memory hook: It sounds a bit like “put a stitch” — imagine stitching together memories on a long journey!  
Repeat after me: путешествие… путешествие.  
- Russian (Cyrillic): билет
  Transliteration: bee-LYET  
  English: ticket  
  Example sentence: Мне нужен билет в Москву.  
  Example translation: I need a ticket to Moscow.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “bee yet” — the bee hasn’t left yet because it needs its ticket!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): чемодан
  Transliteration: cheh-mah-DAHN  
  English: suitcase  
  Example sentence: Чемодан тяжёлый.  
  Example translation: The suitcase is heavy.  
  Memory hook: Remember “тяжёлый” from before? Now your чемодан is full of it!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): паспорт
  Transliteration: PAHS-port  
  English: passport  
  Example sentence: Покажи паспорт.  
  Example translation: Show your passport.  
  Memory hook: It’s almost the same as English “passport” — easy win!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): отель
  Transliteration: ah-TEL  
  English: hotel  
  Example sentence: Мы живём в отеле.  
  Example translation: We live in a hotel.  
  Memory hook: “A tel” sounds like “a tell” — the hotel will tell you where to go!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): самолёт
  Transliteration: sah-mah-LYOT  
  English: airplane  
  Example sentence: Самолёт летает.  
  Example translation: The airplane flies.  
  Memory hook: Remember “летает” from earlier? The самолёт does exactly that!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): вокзал
  Transliteration: vok-ZAHL  
  English: train station  
  Example sentence: Поезд на вокзале.  
  Example translation: The train is at the station.  
  Memory hook: “Vok” like “vocal” — the station is full of vocal announcements!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): рюкзак
  Transliteration: ryook-ZAHK  
  English: backpack  
  Example sentence: Рюкзак на спине.  
  Example translation: The backpack is on the back.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “rook sack” — a rook bird carrying a sack on its back!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): карта
  Transliteration: KAR-tah  
  English: map  
  Example sentence: Дай мне карту.  
  Example translation: Give me the map.  
  Memory hook: Same as “card” — your карта shows the cards of the land!  

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Today we look at the preposition “в” when talking about going somewhere. In Russian you say “в Москву” (to Moscow) or “в отель” (to the hotel). It works like English “to” but the noun often changes its ending. Examples: Я еду в Москву. / Мы идём в отель. Unlike English, Russian uses this little word to show direction, so the city or place gets a special ending.  

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: паспорт**
Did you know that the Russian word паспорт and the English word “passport” are actually the same word? They both come from the French “passeport,” which literally meant “pass through the port.” This word started in medieval French, travelled across Europe with traders and sailors, and landed in Russian in the 1700s when Peter the Great opened Russia to the world. But be careful — the Russian word “магазин” sounds like “magazine” but actually means “shop”! Next time you see your English passport, remember it’s cousins with Russian паспорт — they both come from the idea of safely passing through a port. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.  

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians love long train journeys across their huge country. The famous Trans-Siberian Railway takes seven days from Moscow to Vladivostok, and families often bring big чемоданы full of food for the trip.  

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a picture of your dream trip and label the самолёт, рюкзак, and карта in Russian. For adults: Imagine you’re at the airport — practice saying “Мне нужен билет” and “Покажи паспорт” out loud three times.

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Дерево** (DEH-reh-voh) — tree
Example sentence: Это большое дерево. (EH-toh BOL-shoye DEH-reh-voh.) — This is a big tree.  
Memory hook: Picture a tall “derevo” tree waving its branches like a friendly giant in the forest.  
Repeat after me: Дерево… (pause) Дерево!
- Russian (Cyrillic): река
  Transliteration: reh-KAH  
  English: river  
  Example sentence: Река длинная.  
  Example translation: The river is long.  
  Memory hook: “Reh-KAH” sounds like “ray car” racing along the water.

- Russian (Cyrillic): лес
  Transliteration: lyes  
  English: forest  
  Example sentence: В лесу много деревьев.  
  Example translation: There are many trees in the forest.  
  Memory hook: “Lyes” sounds like “leaves” — perfect for a leafy forest!

- Russian (Cyrillic): гора
  Transliteration: gah-RAH  
  English: mountain  
  Example sentence: Гора высокая.  
  Example translation: The mountain is high.  
  Memory hook: Imagine a “gah-RAH” mountain so tall it touches the garage in the sky.

- Russian (Cyrillic): цветок
  Transliteration: tsvye-TOK  
  English: flower  
  Example sentence: Цветок красивый.  
  Example translation: The flower is beautiful.  
  Memory hook: “Tsvye-TOK” starts with the sound of “tsvet” (color) — flowers bring color!

- Russian (Cyrillic): птица
  Transliteration: PTEE-tsah  
  English: bird  
  Example sentence: Птица летает.  
  Example translation: The bird is flying.  
  Memory hook: Remember “птица” sounds like “peetsa” — a bird that could deliver pizza!

- Russian (Cyrillic): рыба
  Transliteration: RY-bah  
  English: fish  
  Example sentence: Рыба плавает в реке.  
  Example translation: The fish swims in the river.  
  Memory hook: “RY-bah” rhymes with “riba” — think of a riba fish wiggling its ribs.

- Russian (Cyrillic): небо
  Transliteration: NYE-boh  
  English: sky  
  Example sentence: Небо синее.  
  Example translation: The sky is blue.  
  Memory hook: “NYE-boh” sounds like “knee bow” — bow to the beautiful sky!

- Russian (Cyrillic): трава
  Transliteration: trah-VAH  
  English: grass  
  Example sentence: Трава зелёная.  
  Example translation: The grass is green.  
  Memory hook: “Trah-VAH” feels like “traverse” the grass on a walk.

- Russian (Cyrillic): озеро
  Transliteration: OH-zeh-roh  
  English: lake  
  Example sentence: Озеро большое.  
  Example translation: The lake is big.  
  Memory hook: “OH-zeh-roh” sounds like “oh zero” — zero waves on a calm lake.

- Russian (Cyrillic): камень
  Transliteration: KAH-men  
  English: stone / rock  
  Example sentence: Камень тяжёлый.  
  Example translation: The stone is heavy.  
  Memory hook: “KAH-men” sounds like “common” — a common rock on the path.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Adjectives must match the gender of the noun they describe. Russian nouns have genders (masculine, feminine, neuter), and adjectives change their endings.  
- Большое дерево (neuter — ends in -ое)
- Длинная река (feminine — ends in -ая)
- Высокая гора (feminine — ends in -ая)
Unlike English, where adjectives stay the same (“big tree,” “big river”), Russian makes the adjective “agree” so the sentence sounds natural.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: цветок**
Did you know that the Russian word цветок and the English word “color” are actually cousins? They both come from the ancient Proto-Indo-European root *kʷeyt- meaning “to shine” or “bright.” This word started in early Indo-European languages, travelled through Slavic tongues where it became “tsvet” (color), and finally grew into “tsvetok” (flower) because flowers are nature’s brightest colors. But be careful — the Russian word “цвет” sounds like it could mean “color” in English, yet it truly means both color and the blooming flower itself! Next time you see a colorful flower, remember it’s cousins with “цветок” — they both come from that shining root. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians have a deep love for nature and often spend weekends in the лес or at an озеро. Many traditional songs and poems celebrate the красота (beauty) of the Russian landscape, especially the белые берёзы (white birches) that appear in famous paintings and fairy tales.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a simple picture of a лес with a река and three цветки, then label each in Russian and say the words out loud.  
For adults: Look out your window or go for a short walk and describe three things you see using today’s words (for example: “Это дерево” or “Небо синее”).

> **Today we’re heading to the Russian магазин to unlock shopping words that turn every trip into a language adventure!**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
магазин  
Transliteration: ma-ga-ZEEN  
English meaning: store / shop  
Simple example sentence: Я иду в магазин. (Ya ee-DU v ma-ga-ZEEN.) — I am going to the store.  
Memorable hook: It sounds like “magazine,” but it means the place where you buy things!  
Repeat after me: ma-ga-ZEEN… ma-ga-ZEEN.
- Russian (Cyrillic): купить
  Transliteration: ku-PEET’  
  English: to buy  
  Example sentence: Я хочу купить хлеб.  
  Example translation: I want to buy bread.  
  Memory hook: Think “buy it” — ку-пить sounds like “coo-peet” for “buy it quick!”
- Russian (Cyrillic): деньги
  Transliteration: DYEN-ghee  
  English: money  
  Example sentence: У меня есть деньги.  
  Example translation: I have money.  
  Memory hook: “Dime” + “gee” — your money jingles!
- Russian (Cyrillic): цена
  Transliteration: tse-NA  
  English: price  
  Example sentence: Какая цена?  
  Example translation: What is the price?  
  Memory hook: “Tsar” + “nah” — the tsar sets the price!
- Russian (Cyrillic): сумка
  Transliteration: SOOM-ka  
  English: bag  
  Example sentence: У меня большая сумка.  
  Example translation: I have a big bag.  
  Memory hook: “Zoom” your bag home!
- Russian (Cyrillic): платить
  Transliteration: pla-TEET’  
  English: to pay  
  Example sentence: Я плачу за молоко.  
  Example translation: I pay for the milk.  
  Memory hook: “Pla” for plastic card, “teet” like teeth biting the bill.
- Russian (Cyrillic): продавец
  Transliteration: pro-da-VYETS  
  English: seller / shop assistant  
  Example sentence: Продавец помогает мне.  
  Example translation: The seller helps me.  
  Memory hook: “Pro” seller who “da-vyets” you what you need.
- Russian (Cyrillic): корзина
  Transliteration: kar-ZEE-na  
  English: basket / cart  
  Example sentence: Положи фрукты в корзину.  
  Example translation: Put the fruit in the basket.  
  Memory hook: Remember фрукты? Put them in the “car-zee-na” cart!
- Russian (Cyrillic): скидка
  Transliteration: SKEED-ka  
  English: discount  
  Example sentence: Есть скидка на этот товар.  
  Example translation: There is a discount on this item.  
  Memory hook: “Skeed” like speed — prices go down fast!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
The verb “to buy” (купить) changes depending on who is doing the action. In Russian we say я куплю (I will buy), ты купишь (you will buy), он/она купит (he/she will buy). Unlike English, the ending of the verb tells us who is acting — no need for extra words like “I” or “you” every time. Compare: English keeps “I buy,” but Russian changes куплю to show “I.”

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: магазин**
Did you know that the Russian word магазин and the English word “magazine” are actually the same word? They both come from the Arabic “makhazin,” meaning storehouses or shops. This word started in Arabic, travelled through Italian and French as “magasin,” and finally arrived in Russian in the 18th century. But be careful — the Russian word “магазин” sounds like “magazine” but actually means “shop”! Next time you see a magazine on a shelf, remember it’s cousins with магазин — they both come from the same Arabic root for storing goods. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, many people still love outdoor markets called “rynok” where they can buy fresh fruits, vegetables, and homemade goods directly from farmers. These markets are lively places full of friendly bargaining and tasting samples, showing how shopping is also a social event.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a big shopping basket and fill it with pictures of things you would buy, saying each Russian word out loud as you add it. For adults: Next time you go to a store, practice saying “Сколько стоит?” (How much does it cost?) when you see a price tag.

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**яблоко**
Transliteration: YÁ-blah-kah  
English meaning: apple  
Simple example sentence: Я ем яблоко. (Ya yem YÁ-blah-kah.) — I eat an apple.  
Memorable hook: Picture a shiny red яблоко rolling off the table like a bouncy ball!  
Repeat after me: YÁ-blah-kah… YÁ-blah-kah… now faster: яблоко!
- Russian (Cyrillic): молоко
  Transliteration: mah-lah-KÓ  
  English: milk  
  Example sentence: Я пью молоко.  
  Example translation: I drink milk.  
  Memory hook: “Moo-lah-KO” sounds like a cow saying “moo” while drinking milk!
- Russian (Cyrillic): сыр
  Transliteration: syr  
  English: cheese  
  Example sentence: Сыр вкусный.  
  Example translation: The cheese is delicious.  
  Memory hook: “Syr” rhymes with “stir” — stir the cheese into your pasta!
- Russian (Cyrillic): мясо
  Transliteration: MYÁ-sah  
  English: meat  
  Example sentence: Мясо на тарелке.  
  Example translation: Meat is on the plate.  
  Memory hook: Think “my-ah-sah” like “my awesome sausage”!
- Russian (Cyrillic): овощ
  Transliteration: OH-vahshch  
  English: vegetable  
  Example sentence: Овощ зелёный.  
  Example translation: The vegetable is green.  
  Memory hook: “Oh-vash” sounds like “oh, fresh!” veggies from the garden.
- Russian (Cyrillic): фрукт
  Transliteration: frookt  
  English: fruit  
  Example sentence: Фрукт сладкий.  
  Example translation: The fruit is sweet.  
  Memory hook: Remember фрукты from a few lessons ago? It means fruits — now you know the singular фрукт!
- Russian (Cyrillic): есть
  Transliteration: yest’  
  English: to eat  
  Example sentence: Я есть яблоко.  
  Example translation: I eat an apple.  
  Memory hook: “Yest” sounds exactly like the English word “yes” — yes, I want to eat!
- Russian (Cyrillic): пить
  Transliteration: peet’  
  English: to drink  
  Example sentence: Пить молоко.  
  Example translation: Drink milk.  
  Memory hook: “Peet” like “peat” moss, but you drink instead of planting it.
- Russian (Cyrillic): вкусно
  Transliteration: VKOOS-nah  
  English: delicious / tasty  
  Example sentence: Это вкусно!  
  Example translation: This is delicious!  
  Memory hook: “Vkoos-nah” sounds like “vroom” — your taste buds zoom with joy!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Russian nouns have genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) that affect the ending of words like adjectives. Food words often show this: яблоко ends in -о (neuter), сыр ends in a consonant (masculine), and молоко also ends in -о (neuter). Compare to English, where we don’t change endings for gender — we just say “the red apple” or “the red cheese” without extra letters. Examples: вкусное яблоко (neuter), вкусный сыр (masculine), вкусное молоко (neuter).

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: чай**
Did you know that the Russian word чай and the English word “tea” are actually cousins from the same ancient root? They both come from the Chinese word “chá,” which travelled along the Silk Road — first to Persian and Turkish traders, then into Russian around the 17th century when tea became popular in Moscow. But be careful — the Russian word “магазин” sounds like “magazine” but actually means “shop”! Next time you see “tea” on a menu, remember it’s cousins with чай — they both come from Chinese “chá.” That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, tea (чай) is more than a drink — it’s a daily ritual shared with family and friends, often served with jam, lemon, or sweets in a special teapot called a samovar. Offering tea to guests is a warm sign of hospitality that has lasted for centuries.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your favourite Russian food (like an яблоко or сыр) and label it with the Russian word, then say “Это вкусно!” out loud. For adults: Next time you’re in a café, practise ordering by saying “Я хочу [food] и молоко, пожалуйста” — try it with a friend!

> **Today we step outside into the wild Russian weather to learn words that let you describe sun, rain, wind, and snow like a local.**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Солнце** (SOHL-ntseh) — sun
Example sentence: Солнце светит ярко. (The sun shines brightly.)  
Memory hook: Picture the sun as a big golden “soul” warming everything — “solntse” sounds like “soul” and brings the same bright feeling!  
Repeat after me: Солнце… (pause) Солнце светит ярко.
- Russian (Cyrillic): ветер
  Transliteration: VYEH-ter  
  English: wind  
  Example sentence: Ветер дует сильно.  
  Example translation: The wind blows strongly.  
  Memory hook: “Veter” sounds like “veteran” — imagine a tough old wind that has been blowing for years.
- Russian (Cyrillic): дождь
  Transliteration: DOZH-d’  
  English: rain  
  Example sentence: Дождь идёт.  
  Example translation: It is raining.  
  Memory hook: Remember “дождь” from earlier — it sounds a bit like “drench,” which is exactly what rain does!
- Russian (Cyrillic): снег
  Transliteration: S’NYEK  
  English: snow  
  Example sentence: Снег белый и холодный.  
  Example translation: Snow is white and cold.  
  Memory hook: “S’nyek” rhymes with “neck” — picture snowflakes tickling your neck.
- Russian (Cyrillic): облако
  Transliteration: OB-la-ka  
  English: cloud  
  Example sentence: Облако плывёт по небу.  
  Example translation: The cloud floats across the sky.  
  Memory hook: “Oblako” sounds like “obstacle” — clouds can block the sun like an obstacle.
- Russian (Cyrillic): тепло
  Transliteration: tyep-LO  
  English: warm / warmth  
  Example sentence: Сегодня тепло.  
  Example translation: It is warm today.  
  Memory hook: “Teplo” sounds like “tepid” but means pleasantly warm.
- Russian (Cyrillic): холодно
  Transliteration: ha-LOHD-na  
  English: cold  
  Example sentence: На улице холодно.  
  Example translation: It is cold outside.  
  Memory hook: “Kholodno” starts like “cold” — perfect match!
- Russian (Cyrillic): гроза
  Transliteration: gra-ZA  
  English: thunderstorm  
  Example sentence: Гроза идёт.  
  Example translation: A thunderstorm is coming.  
  Memory hook: “Groza” sounds like “grows a” storm — it grows louder and louder.
- Russian (Cyrillic): радуга
  Transliteration: RAH-du-ga  
  English: rainbow  
  Example sentence: После дождя появляется радуга.  
  Example translation: After the rain a rainbow appears.  
  Memory hook: “Raduga” sounds like “rad” (happy) + “uga” — a happy arc in the sky.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, weather often uses impersonal constructions with “it” understood but not said. “Сегодня тепло” literally means “Today [is] warm” — no subject needed. Compare to English “It is warm today.”  
Examples:  
- Холодно. (It is cold.)
- Дождь идёт. (Rain goes = It is raining.)
- Ветер сильный. (Wind [is] strong.)

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: ветер**
Did you know that the Russian word ветер and the English word “wind” are actually cousins from the same ancient root? They both come from the Proto-Indo-European *weh- meaning “to blow.” This word started in that ancient language, travelled through Germanic tongues to become English “wind,” and through Slavic branches to become Russian ветер.  
But be careful — the Russian word “ветер” sounds nothing like the false friend “weather,” which in Russian is actually погода!  
Next time you feel the wind on your face, remember it is cousins with ветер — they both come from the same blowing root. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians love talking about the weather because it changes dramatically across their huge country — from snowy winters in Siberia to sunny summers in the south. People often greet each other with “Как погода?” (“How is the weather?”) as a friendly way to start a conversation.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a picture of today’s weather and label the sun, clouds, and wind in Russian, then say the words out loud.  
For adults: Step outside or look out the window and describe the weather in one simple Russian sentence using today’s words.

> **Today we’re roaring, barking, and chirping our way through the animal kingdom to unlock the Russian words that let you talk about every creature from pets to polar bears!**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Собака** (so-BA-ka) — dog
Example sentence: Моя собака любит бегать. (My dog loves to run.)  
Memory hook: Imagine a Siberian husky barking “so-BA-ka!” like it’s calling its own name.  
Repeat after me: So-BA-ka… so-BA-ka… now faster: собака!
- **Собака** (so-BA-ka) — dog
  Example sentence: Собака играет во дворе.  
  Example translation: The dog is playing in the yard.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “so bark-a” — perfect for a barking dog!

- **Медведь** (myed-VYED’) — bear
  Example sentence: Большой медведь спит в лесу.  
  Example translation: The big bear sleeps in the forest.  
  Memory hook: Think “my head” with a “vyed” growl at the end — a bear with a big head!

- **Птица** (PTI-tsa) — bird
  Example sentence: Птица поёт на дереве.  
  Example translation: The bird sings in the tree.  
  Memory hook: “Ptee-tsa” flits like a tweet from a tiny bird.

- **Рыба** (RY-ba) — fish
  Example sentence: Рыба плавает в воде.  
  Example translation: The fish swims in the water.  
  Memory hook: “Ree-ba” rhymes with “reefer” — a fish in the reef!

- **Лошадь** (LO-shad’) — horse
  Example sentence: Лошадь бежит быстро.  
  Example translation: The horse runs fast.  
  Memory hook: “Lo-shad” sounds like “low shed” where a horse might hide.

- **Мышь** (MYSH) — mouse
  Example sentence: Маленькая мышь ест сыр.  
  Example translation: The little mouse eats cheese.  
  Memory hook: Remember мышь from before? It still means mouse — tiny and quick!

- **Кот** (kot) — tomcat / male cat
  Example sentence: Кот сидит на окне.  
  Example translation: The cat sits on the window.  
  Memory hook: “Kot” is short and cozy, like a cat curled up.

- **Заяц** (ZA-yats) — hare / rabbit
  Example sentence: Заяц прыгает в поле.  
  Example translation: The hare jumps in the field.  
  Memory hook: “Za-yats” sounds like “za-yachts” racing across a field.

- **Лев** (lyef) — lion
  Example sentence: Лев рычит громко.  
  Example translation: The lion roars loudly.  
  Memory hook: “Lyef” is like “leaf” but with a mighty roar instead of rustling.

- **Слон** (slon) — elephant
  Example sentence: Слон пьёт воду хоботом.  
  Example translation: The elephant drinks water with its trunk.  
  Memory hook: “Slon” sounds like “slon-g” — a long trunk swinging like a slingshot!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Russian nouns have genders (masculine, feminine, or neuter) that affect the words around them. Most animal names ending in a consonant like собака’s friend кот are masculine, while птица and мышь are feminine. Compare to English, where we rarely mark gender on nouns — in Russian you say “большой кот” (big tomcat) but “большая птица” (big bird). Practice: мой кот (my cat, masculine) vs. моя рыба (my fish, feminine).

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: Медведь**
Did you know the Russian word медведь and the English idea of “honey-eater” are secretly cousins? This word started in ancient Slavic roots where “мёд” (myod) meant honey and “ведать” meant to know — so медведь literally means “the one who knows honey,” a polite way to avoid saying the real bear name and angering the animal! It travelled through old Slavic languages without borrowing from Latin “ursus” like most European tongues. But be careful — the Russian word “медведь” sounds nothing like English “bear,” yet both cultures used sweet nicknames to talk about the scary forest giant. Next time you see honey, remember it’s cousins with медведь — they both come from the same sweet Slavic secret.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russian fairy tales, animals often act like wise teachers or tricky helpers — the bear is strong but kind, the fox is clever, and the wolf can be both scary and funny. Kids grow up hearing stories like “The Bear and the Fox” that teach lessons through animal adventures, just like Aesop’s fables but with snowy forests and magic.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your favourite animal from today’s list and label it with the Russian word — then roar, bark, or chirp the word three times! For adults: Look at a pet photo or zoo picture and say three full sentences using today’s words, like “Это собака. Она бежит.” (This is a dog. She is running.)

> **Today we unlock the magic of Russian feelings so you can say exactly how happy, tired, or excited you are!**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**счастливый** (schastlivy) — happy
Example sentence: Я счастливый! (Ya schastlivy!) — I am happy!  
Memory hook: It sounds a bit like “chest of liveliness” — picture your chest filling with joy!  
Repeat after me: schast-lee-vy… schastlivy!
- Russian (Cyrillic): грустный
  Transliteration: grustny  
  English: sad  
  Example sentence: Кот грустный.  
  Example translation: The cat is sad.  
  Memory hook: “Grr” + “sad” = the sound you make when you feel down.

- Russian (Cyrillic): устал
  Transliteration: ustal  
  English: tired  
  Example sentence: Я устал после школы.  
  Example translation: I am tired after school.  
  Memory hook: “U-stall” — you stall when you’re too tired to move.

- Russian (Cyrillic): весёлый
  Transliteration: vyesyoly  
  English: cheerful / merry  
  Example sentence: Друг весёлый.  
  Example translation: My friend is cheerful.  
  Memory hook: “Ves-yo-ly” sounds like “very jolly.”

- Russian (Cyrillic): злой
  Transliteration: zloy  
  English: angry  
  Example sentence: Он злой сегодня.  
  Example translation: He is angry today.  
  Memory hook: “Zloy” rhymes with “toy” — imagine an angry toy stomping.

- Russian (Cyrillic): испуганный
  Transliteration: ispuganny  
  English: scared  
  Example sentence: Мышь испуганная.  
  Example translation: The mouse is scared.  
  Memory hook: “Is-poo-gan” — you get the “poo” scared out of you!

- Russian (Cyrillic): спокойный
  Transliteration: spokoyny  
  English: calm  
  Example sentence: Мама спокойная.  
  Example translation: Mom is calm.  
  Memory hook: “Spo-koy-ny” sounds like “so quiet.”

- Russian (Cyrillic): Я чувствую…
  Transliteration: Ya chuvstvuyu…  
  English: I feel…  
  Example sentence: Я чувствую радость.  
  Example translation: I feel joy.  
  Memory hook: “Chuv-stvuyu” = “choose to feel you.”

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, adjectives like счастливый, грустный, and усталый change their ending to match the gender of the noun or person they describe. For a boy or “I” (male speaker) we say счастливый; for a girl we say счастливая. It’s like English “happy” vs “happier,” but here the ending tells us who is feeling the emotion.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: счастливый**
Did you know that the Russian word счастливый and the English word “happy” are actually cousins through an ancient root? This word started in Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje meaning “good fortune,” travelled through Old Church Slavonic, and finally settled in modern Russian. But be careful — the similar-sounding English “chest” has nothing to do with it; счастливый comes from “part” or “share” of luck! Next time you feel happy, remember it’s cousins with счастливый — they both come from the idea of sharing good fortune. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians often say “Как дела?” (How are things?) not just as a greeting but because sharing feelings is part of warm, honest conversation. In Russian families, children are encouraged to name their emotions openly, just like we do today.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a face showing each feeling (happy, sad, tired) and label it with the Russian word.  
For adults: Tonight at dinner, tell a family member “Я счастливый/грустный/устал” in Russian and explain why in one simple sentence.

English meaning: school

  Example translation: The children are writing.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, many verbs change their ending depending on who is doing the action. For “to read,” we say я читаю (ya chitáyu — I read) but он читает (on chitáyet — he reads). It is like English “I read” vs. “he reads,” but Russian changes the ending every time. Listen: я читаю… он читает. Try it: ya chitáyu… on chitáyet.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: книга**
Did you know that the Russian word книга and the English word “book” are actually cousins through an ancient journey? This word started in ancient Greek as “biblion,” travelled through Old Church Slavonic, and finally settled in Russian centuries ago. Along the way it picked up the soft “kn” sound we hear today. But be careful — the Russian word “книга” looks nothing like “book,” yet both mean the same thing and share that hidden Greek root! Next time you open a book, remember its Russian cousin книга — they both come from the same ancient word for “papyrus scroll.” That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, children start school at age six or seven and often stay in the same class with the same teacher for the first four years. This creates a very close “family” feeling inside the classroom, and kids celebrate the first day of school, called “День знаний,” with big bouquets of flowers for their teachers.

**Practice Challenge:**

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**самолёт**
**Transliteration:** sa-mo-LYOT
**English meaning:** airplane
**Example sentence:** Я лечу на самолёте в Москву.
**Example translation:** I am flying to Moscow on an airplane.
Imagine a “samolyot” soaring like a silver bird — the word even sounds like it’s zooming through the sky!
**Repeat after me:** sa-mo-LYOT… sa-mo-LYOT… now say it fast: самолёт!
- Russian (Cyrillic): билет
  Transliteration: bi-LYET  
  English: ticket  
  Example sentence: Дай мне билет, пожалуйста.  
  Example translation: Give me a ticket, please.  
  Memory hook: “Billet” sounds like “bill-et” — your ticket is the bill that lets you ride!

- Russian (Cyrillic): вокзал
  Transliteration: vok-ZAL  
  English: train station  
  Example sentence: Где вокзал?  
  Example translation: Where is the train station?  
  Memory hook: “Vokzal” is like “vocal” but for trains — listen for the loud announcements!

- Russian (Cyrillic): чемодан
  Transliteration: che-mo-DAN  
  English: suitcase  
  Example sentence: Мой чемодан тяжёлый.  
  Example translation: My suitcase is heavy.  
  Memory hook: Think “chemo-dan” carrying your clothes like a portable closet.

- Russian (Cyrillic): паспорт
  Transliteration: PAS-port  
  English: passport  
  Example sentence: Покажи паспорт.  
  Example translation: Show your passport.  
  Memory hook: Same word in English — easy win!

- Russian (Cyrillic): аэропорт
  Transliteration: a-e-ro-PORT  
  English: airport  
  Example sentence: Мы в аэропорту.  
  Example translation: We are at the airport.  
  Memory hook: “Aero-port” — air + port = where planes land.

- Russian (Cyrillic): путешествие
  Transliteration: pu-te-SHEST-vi-ye  
  English: journey / trip  
  Example sentence: Путешествие в Россию весёлое.  
  Example translation: The trip to Russia is fun.  
  Memory hook: “Pute-shest” sounds like “put a chest” of adventures in your suitcase.

- Russian (Cyrillic): такси
  Transliteration: tak-SEE  
  English: taxi  
  Example sentence: Позови такси.  
  Example translation: Call a taxi.  
  Memory hook: Same as English “taxi” — instant friend!

- Russian (Cyrillic): отель
  Transliteration: o-TEL  
  English: hotel  
  Example sentence: Отель рядом с вокзалом.  
  Example translation: The hotel is near the train station.  
  Memory hook: “O-tel” like “hotel” without the H.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
The question word “где” (where) helps you find places while traveling. It usually comes at the start of a question.  
Examples: Где вокзал? (Where is the train station?) Где мой чемодан? (Where is my suitcase?)  
In English we also start with “where,” but Russian often drops the verb “is” — so “Где вокзал?” is shorter and snappier than “Where is the train station?”

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: билет**
Did you know the Russian word билет and the English word “ticket” are actually cousins from the same French root? They both come from the Old French “billet,” meaning a short note or document. This word started in Latin as “bulla” (a seal or document), travelled through French, and arrived in Russian in the 1700s when Peter the Great opened Russia to European travel. But be careful — a false friend lurks nearby: Russian “билет” can also mean an exam “ticket” or test paper, not just travel! Next time you buy a ticket, remember it’s cousins with билет — they both come from the same Latin seal, your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, long train journeys are a beloved tradition — people bring tea in special glasses with metal holders and chat for hours. The famous Trans-Siberian Railway crosses eight time zones, making it the ultimate adventure!

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a big airplane and label it самолёт, then add a suitcase (чемодан) and a ticket (билет) — color them and say each word out loud!  
For adults: Next time you book travel, practice saying “Билет, пожалуйста” and “Где вокзал?” in front of a mirror. Remember дом from earlier lessons? Imagine leaving your дом, grabbing фрукты for the trip, and asking где the platform when boarding поезде!

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**семья**
Transliteration: sem-YA  
English meaning: family  
Example sentence: Это моя семья. (Eto moya sem'ya.)  
English translation: This is my family.  
Memory hook: It sounds like “seminar” but means the people you gather with every day.  
Repeat after me: сем…ья… сем…ья… семья!
- Russian (Cyrillic): мама
  Transliteration: MA-ma  
  English: mom  
  Example sentence: Моя мама любит читать.  
  Example translation: My mom loves to read.  
  Memory hook: Same as English “mama” — the very first word most babies say!

- Russian (Cyrillic): папа
  Transliteration: PA-pa  
  English: dad  
  Example sentence: Папа работает.  
  Example translation: Dad is working.  
  Memory hook: Exactly like “papa” — easy to remember!

- Russian (Cyrillic): брат
  Transliteration: brat  
  English: brother  
  Example sentence: У меня есть брат.  
  Example translation: I have a brother.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “brat” but means the opposite — your helpful sibling!

- Russian (Cyrillic): сестра
  Transliteration: ses-TRA  
  English: sister  
  Example sentence: Моя сестра играет.  
  Example translation: My sister is playing.  
  Memory hook: “Ses” like “sister” + “tra” at the end.

- Russian (Cyrillic): бабушка
  Transliteration: BAB-ush-ka  
  English: grandmother  
  Example sentence: Бабушка печёт пироги.  
  Example translation: Grandma bakes pies.  
  Memory hook: “Babushka” is the famous Russian word for grandma — say it with a smile!

- Russian (Cyrillic): дедушка
  Transliteration: DED-ush-ka  
  English: grandfather  
  Example sentence: Дедушка рассказывает истории.  
  Example translation: Grandpa tells stories.  
  Memory hook: “Ded” like “dad” + “ushka” makes it grandpa.

- Russian (Cyrillic): дочь
  Transliteration: doch’  
  English: daughter  
  Example sentence: Моя дочь любит кошку.  
  Example translation: My daughter loves the cat.  
  Memory hook: “Doch” rhymes with “dough” — the girl who makes the family dough rise with joy!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, words for family members often change ending to show “my” or “your.” We add -а or -я for “my.”  
Examples:  
моя мама (moya mama) — my mom  
мой папа (moy papa) — my dad  
моя сестра (moya sestra) — my sister  
English does the same with “my,” but Russian makes the ending match the person’s gender.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: мама**
Did you know that the Russian word мама and the English word mama are actually the same word? They both come from the very first sounds babies make all over the world. This word started as a natural baby sound, travelled through ancient languages, and settled into both Russian and English with almost no change. But be careful — the Russian word “папа” sounds exactly like English “papa,” yet in some languages it can mean something else entirely! Next time you hear “mama,” remember it’s cousins with Russian мама — they both come from the universal first word babies say. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, бабушки often play a very active role in raising grandchildren, helping with school and cooking big Sunday meals. Families love to gather around the table for long talks and tea, making “семья” feel like the heart of daily life.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your семья and label each person with the new Russian words, then say each name out loud.  
For adults: Introduce your family in one sentence using “моя” or “мой,” for example: “Моя мама и мой папа живут в доме.” Remember дом from a few lessons ago? That’s the house where your семья lives!

English meaning: bread

- Russian (Cyrillic): молоко

- Russian (Cyrillic): сыр

- Russian (Cyrillic): суп

  English: soup  
  Example sentence: Горячий суп.

- Russian (Cyrillic): чай

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Russian nouns have genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) that affect the words around them.  
- Хлеб is masculine, so we say “вкусный хлеб.”
- Яблоко is neuter, so we say “вкусное яблоко.”
- Compare to English: we don’t change adjectives for gender, but in Russian it’s like giving every noun its own “team colour.”

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: чай**
Did you know that the Russian word чай and the English word “tea” are actually cousins from the same ancient root? This word started in China as “cha,” travelled along the Silk Road through Persian and Turkish traders, and finally arrived in Russian in the 17th century when tea became popular at the royal court. But be careful — the Russian word “магазин” sounds like “magazine” but actually means “shop”! Next time you sip a cup of tea, remember its cousin чай — they both come from the same Chinese root. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, bread is treated with great respect — it is often placed in the centre of the table and people say “хлеб — всему голова” (bread is the head of everything). Guests are traditionally welcomed with bread and salt, showing warmth and hospitality.

# Привет, Русский! — Episode Plan

### Word of the Day
**Дождь** (dozhd') — rain
Example sentence: Дождь идёт. (Dozhd' idyot.) — It is raining.  
Memory hook: Imagine “drizzle” turning into “dozhd'” — both start with that soft “d” sound and bring water from the sky!  
Repeat after me: Dozhd'... dozhd'!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Солнце
  Transliteration: Solntse  
  English: Sun  
  Example sentence: Солнце светит.  
  Example translation: The sun is shining.  
  Memory hook: “Solntse” sounds like “sun” but with a cheerful Russian ending — picture a big yellow ball smiling down!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Снег
  Transliteration: Sneg  
  English: Snow  
  Example sentence: Снег белый.  
  Example translation: The snow is white.  
  Memory hook: “Sneg” rhymes with “leg” — think of cold white flakes landing on your leg!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Ветер
  Transliteration: Veter  
  English: Wind  
  Example sentence: Ветер дует.  
  Example translation: The wind is blowing.  
  Memory hook: “Veter” sounds like “veteran” but means the air moving fast — a veteran wind that has travelled far!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Небо
  Transliteration: Nebo  
  English: Sky  
  Example sentence: Небо голубое.  
  Example translation: The sky is blue.  
  Memory hook: “Nebo” is like “nebula” — both mean the big open space above us!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Тепло
  Transliteration: Teplo  
  English: Warm  
  Example sentence: Сегодня тепло.  
  Example translation: It is warm today.  
  Memory hook: “Teplo” sounds like “tepid” but means pleasantly warm — perfect for a sunny day!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Холодно
  Transliteration: Kholodno  
  English: Cold  
  Example sentence: Зимой холодно.  
  Example translation: It is cold in winter.  
  Memory hook: “Kholodno” starts like “cold” — easy to remember when you feel a chilly breeze!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Радуга (review from earlier)
  Transliteration: Raduga  
  English: Rainbow  
  Example sentence: После дождя радуга.  
  Example translation: After the rain there is a rainbow.  
  Memory hook: Remember “raduga” means rainbow — it appears when sun meets rain!
- Russian (Cyrillic): Мой (review)
  Transliteration: Moy  
  English: My  
  Example sentence: Мой дом.  
  Example translation: My house.  
  Memory hook: “Moy” sounds like “my” — your own personal weather word!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Adjectives must match the gender of the noun they describe. In Russian, “небо” (sky) is neuter, so we say “голубое небо” (blue sky). “Дождь” (rain) is masculine, so “сильный дождь” (strong rain). English does not change adjective endings, but Russian adds -ое, -ый, or -ая to show the match — a small ending that makes your sentences sound correct!

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: Небо**
Did you know that the Russian word “небо” and the English word “nebula” are actually the same word? They both come from the ancient Latin “nebula,” meaning cloud or mist. This word started in Latin, travelled through scientific writing into English as “nebula” for starry clouds, and stayed in Russian as the everyday word for the sky above us. But be careful — the Russian word “небо” also means “heaven,” creating a lovely double meaning that English keeps separate! Next time you look up at the sky, remember “небо” is cousins with “nebula” — they both come from the same misty Latin root. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians love talking about the weather because winters are long and cold while summers can be hot and sunny. People often greet each other with “Как погода?” (How is the weather?) and use it as a friendly way to start a conversation, just like saying hello!

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a picture of today’s weather and label the sun, rain, or snow with the Russian words you learned. For adults: Look out the window right now and say one full sentence in Russian about the weather — then repeat it three times!

  Example translation: It is warm today.  
  Memory hook: “Tyep-lo” sounds like “tepid” — pleasantly warm!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): Холодно
  Transliteration: kha-LOHD-na  
  English: cold  
  Example sentence: На улице холодно.  
  Example translation: It is cold outside.  
  Memory hook: “Kha-lod-no” starts like “chilly” — both describe cold days.  

- Russian (Cyrillic): Жара
  Transliteration: zha-RA  
  English: heat / hot weather  
  Example sentence: Летом бывает жара.  
  Example translation: In summer there is heat.  
  Memory hook: “Zha-ra” sounds like “sahara” — hot, hot, hot!  

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Today we look at simple weather sentences using “сегодня” (today) and adjectives. In Russian, adjectives often change their ending to match the noun’s gender.  
Examples:  
- Сегодня тепло. (It is warm today.) — neutral form
- Сегодня жарко. (It is hot today.) — neutral form
- Небо голубое. (The sky is blue.) — “голубое” matches neutral “небо”
Unlike English, Russian makes the adjective “agree” with the noun; English keeps adjectives the same.

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: Солнце**
Did you know that the Russian word солнце and the English word “solar” are actually cousins from the same ancient root? This word started in Proto-Indo-European as *sóh₂wl̥, travelled through ancient Slavic languages, and settled in Russian as солнце while Latin turned it into “sol” and later “solar.”  
But be careful — the Russian word “небо” sounds a little like “nebula” yet simply means “sky,” not a space cloud!  
Next time you see “solar” panels, remember it is cousins with солнце — they both come from the same shining root. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
Russians love discussing the weather because their huge country has everything from Arctic snow to southern heat. In many cities people greet each other with “Как погода?” (How is the weather?) before talking about anything else — it is a warm way to start any conversation.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a picture of today’s weather and label the sun, clouds, or rain with the new Russian words, then say each word out loud.  
For adults: Step outside or look out the window and make one sentence in Russian describing the weather right now — for example “Сегодня тепло” — then repeat it three times.

- Russian (Cyrillic): Жарко
Transliteration: ZHARK-a  
English: hot (weather)  
Example sentence: Сегодня жарко.  
Example translation: It is hot today.  
Memory hook: Feels like "jarring" heat on a summer day.
- Russian (Cyrillic): Холодно
Transliteration: ha-LOHD-na  
English: cold (weather)  
Example sentence: Зимой холодно.  
Example translation: It is cold in winter.

- Russian (Cyrillic): Небо
Transliteration: NYE-ba  
English: sky  
Example sentence: Небо синее.

- Russian (Cyrillic): Погода
Transliteration: pa-GO-da  
English: weather  
Example sentence: Погода хорошая.  
Example translation: The weather is good.

**Grammar Spotlight:**
We are looking at simple present-tense weather sentences using "есть" (to be) implied or "идёт/дует" for actions. Russian often drops the verb "is" in descriptions. Examples: "Солнце светит" (The sun shines), "Дождь идёт" (Rain goes/It rains), "Ветер дует" (Wind blows). Unlike English which always needs "is raining," Russian uses action verbs directly — shorter and punchy!

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: Небо**
Did you know that the Russian word небо and the English word "nebula" are actually cousins from the same ancient root? They both come from the Proto-Indo-European word for "cloud" or "mist" that travelled through Latin and Greek into English scientific terms while staying everyday-simple in Russian. This word started in ancient roots describing the misty dome above, moved through Slavic languages unchanged for centuries, and kept its sky meaning while English cousins turned more starry. But be careful — don't mix it with "heaven" which is "рай" in Russian! Next time you look up at the небо, remember it's linked to nebula — your secret shortcut to picturing the cloudy sky forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia people love talking about the weather because winters are long and snowy while summers can be surprisingly hot. Russians often say "погода шепчет" when the weather is just right for a walk, showing how weather is part of daily chats and nature appreciation.

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a big sun, cloud, and snowflake then label each with the Russian word and say it out loud three times. For adults: Look out the window right now and make one full sentence in Russian about today's погода using two new words!

Did you know that the Russian word медведь and the English idea of “honey-eater” are basically the same word? They both come from an ancient root that meant “honey-knower.”

Next time you see the English word “honey,” remember it’s cousins with медведь — they both come from the same ancient root about sweet golden treats. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

### Word of the Day
Поезд  
Transliteration: poyezd

- Russian (Cyrillic): самолёт
  Transliteration: samolyot

  Example sentence: Самолёт летит высоко.

- Russian (Cyrillic): билет

  Example translation: Where is my ticket?  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “bee-let” — a little bee that lets you on the plane!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): чемодан
  Transliteration: chemodan  
  English: suitcase  
  Example sentence: Мой чемодан тяжёлый.  
  Example translation: My suitcase is heavy.  
  Memory hook: “Chemo-dan” — imagine a “chemical dan” packing his bag!  

- Russian (Cyrillic): вокзал
  Transliteration: vokzal  
  English: train station  
  Example sentence: Мы на вокзале.  
  Example translation: We are at the train station.  
  Memory hook: “Vok-zal” sounds like “walk-zal” — where you walk to catch the train!

  Transliteration: pasport  
  English: passport  
  Example sentence: Покажи паспорт.

  Transliteration: puteshestviye

  Transliteration: karta  
  English: map  
  Example sentence: Дай мне карту.  
  Example translation: Give me the map.  
  Memory hook: Sounds like “cart” — a cart that shows the way!  

**Grammar Spotlight:**
In Russian, many travel words use the preposition “на” (na) to mean “by” or “on” when talking about transport. It works like this: на поезде (by train), на самолёте (by airplane). Unlike English “by,” Russian changes the ending of the word after “на.” Example: Я еду на поезде. (I go by train.) / Мы летим на самолёте. (We fly by airplane.) It is similar to English “on the train” but always uses “на” for vehicles.  

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: билет**
Did you know that the Russian word билет and the English word “ticket” are actually cousins that both come from the same old French root? This word started in Latin as “titulus” meaning a little label or note, travelled through French as “billet,” and arrived in Russian in the 1700s when Peter the Great was modernizing travel. But be careful — the Russian word “билет” can also mean an exam paper in school, so context tells you if it’s for a train or a test! Next time you see a ticket, remember it’s cousins with билет — they both come from that little Latin label. That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.  

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, long train journeys are a beloved tradition. People often bring tea in special glasses with metal holders and chat with strangers in the compartment, turning a simple trip into a warm social experience.  

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw a train, plane, and suitcase, then label each one with the Russian word while saying it out loud. For adults: Imagine you are at the airport — practice saying “Где мой билет?” and “Мой чемодан тяжёлый” to yourself three times.

  Example sentence: Я люблю яблоко. (Ya lyublyu yabloko.)  
  Example translation: I love an apple.  
  Memory hook: “Yabloko” starts like “yap” — a dog might “yap” for an apple!

- Russian (Cyrillic): вода
  Transliteration: voda  
  English: water  
  Example sentence: Пей воду. (Pey vodu.)  
  Example translation: Drink water.  
  Memory hook: “Voda” sounds like “vodka” without the fun part — it’s just plain water.

- Russian (Cyrillic): чай
  Transliteration: chay  
  English: tea  
  Example sentence: Чай горячий. (Chay goryachiy.)

  Memory hook: “Chay” sounds exactly like “chai” in chai tea — you already know it!

  Example sentence: Мясо на тарелке. (Myaso na tarelke.)

  Memory hook: “Myaso” starts like “my” — “my” favourite meat!

- Russian (Cyrillic): есть
  Transliteration: yest’  
  English: to eat  
  Example sentence: Я ем хлеб. (Ya yem khleb.)  
  Example translation: I eat bread.  
  Memory hook: “Yest’” sounds like “yes” — yes, I want to eat!

**Grammar Spotlight:**
Russian nouns have gender — they are masculine, feminine, or neuter. Food words show this clearly: хлеб is masculine (ends in a consonant), молоко is neuter (ends in -о), and вода is feminine (ends in -а). In English we don’t change words this way, but in Russian you must match adjectives to the noun’s gender. Example: вкусный хлеб (masculine), вкусное молоко (neuter), вкусная вода (feminine). The ending of the adjective changes to match!

**Word Origins — Deep Dive: чай**
Did you know that the Russian word чай and the English word “chai” are actually the same word? They both come from the Chinese word for tea, “chá.” This word started in China, travelled along the ancient Silk Road through Central Asia, was borrowed into Russian in the 17th century, and later reached English as “chai” through trade. But be careful — the Russian word “магазин” sounds like “magazine” but actually means “shop”! Next time you see “chai” on a menu, remember it’s cousins with чай — they both come from Chinese “chá.” That connection is your secret shortcut to remembering it forever.

**Cultural Corner:**
In Russia, tea is more than a drink — it is a daily ritual of hospitality. Families gather around the samovar (a special metal urn) to drink strong tea with jam, lemon, or sweets. Offering tea to guests is a warm way to say “you are welcome here.”

**Practice Challenge:**
For kids: Draw your favourite food and label it with the Russian word (try хлеб or яблоко). For adults: Next time you make breakfast, say the Russian names out loud — “Я ем хлеб и пью чай” — while you prepare it.
